sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We were originally going to extend the HVM, but we realized only 2.5 people on our team actually knew rust, which it's written in. Thus one of us sacrificed his honors thesis project idea and now we're doing language-agnostic IPC. In essence, while working with python is great, it is a slow language and it would be great if we can extend the speedyness of C to it. Or, using JavaScript is fun, but what if I want to do machine learning on it without using the infamously bad tensorjs? It would be great if we can design a library that takes care of inter-language function calls with minimal overhead while achieving security, speed, and correctness.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: It allows you to call functions from other languages like you're importing a library. It's as easy as that. Behind the scenes of course it's a bit more complicated than that, we have to establish a socket from the client, send back the function mainfest from the server, then send and receive all the various packets across the socket, but for the end user basically all you have to do is decorate a couple functions and say loadPY("myfile.py") . An example we have is trying to interact with python-native code through Javascript. Imagine you want to jump onto the AI bandwagon and try out the different AI libraries or run a local LLM, but you only know Javascript. Fear not, with onedef, you can call python libraries easier than ever. In our example, the python code loads up a local LLM and we can interact with it via Javascript.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Pure NodeJS and pure python. We used their respective socket libraries and built up everything around it form the ground up. Each language has their corresponding encoding and decoding parts that can invoke a function call in the other language and decipher the results. The demo website is done using express and hosted on an on-demand AWS EC2 instance structured through Terraform.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It was basically impossible to test anything until we had basically all the code in place. This is because in order for us to do anything there were a bunch of handshakes that would happen first and a lot of data exchange over sockets. If you don't have what you're exchanging or don't have the sockets set up yet then it's hard to test one without the other. We also had issues with python asyncio--it's truly the worst async functionality any language provides. AWS CLI is also very unforgiving when it comes to trying to SSH into the server to have it host our website, we ran into multiple errors surrounding SSH keys and SSH timeouts.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We have full python-JavaScript interoperability. You can use either as a client and the other as a server. Heck, you could even use either of them as a server. We also have a very robust package spec, which while was non-trivial to encode and decode, is very efficient (we don't just send JSON back and forth lol). We are also proud that we were able successfully use a IaC tool, Terraform, and set up an EC2 instance to host our website within the time constraint.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned recursive C macros, UNIX domain sockets, sockets in general, sockets in specific, python async, and how to stay awake for 24 hours straight. We learned to work with binaries, encoding data and data types into their corresponding binaries to follow a IPC protocol. Having to encode arrays, we also learned to deal with writing complex recursive algorithms. We also learned how to create EC2 instances using Terraform and being able to work with SSH keys to remotely access the EC2 instance we created (without touching the AWS EC2 Console at all!)

sections.heading: What's next for onedef
sections.text: More languages! First on the list is C, then maybe Rust. These languages aren't totally trivial to just pump out so we could only finish two for this hackathon, but this IPC spec is portable to any language. We could also absolutely swap out our UNIX domain sockets for TCP sockets and have it act as a websocket. Eventually, it can be implemented for all languages and there will be very minimal overhead for programmers to enjoy the inter-langiage capabilities they will grasp on their hands.

devpost_page.tagline: AR glasses for physical work. It sees what you see, hears what you hear, and gives real-time responses to help you build anything.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Last year, the US had a shortage of 70,000 electricians and 642,000 mechanics. With one in five of these tradespeople over the age of 55 and growing demand in data centers and electric vehicles, this gap is only getting bigger. But what if everyone could become a skilled technician in under 5 minutes? This is why we built Bob. By using this AI+AR assistant, homeowners could handle simple repairs, vocational schools could train workers more efficiently, and professionals could work faster, safer, and more collaboratively.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Bob is a pair of agentic AR glasses that automatically watches over your actions, listens to your questions, and responds to your needs in real time. This could be instructions for your next steps, object-specific details (like a resistor's resistance), or warnings before you do something dangerous. For complex, collaborative tasks, it can also contact your teammates or highlight selected objects (in case you don't know what a “Kellum grip” is). While existing smart glasses focus on specific workflows like trivia or design, we built Bob to be a generalist from the outset. It can help you build electrical circuits, repair cars, and assemble furniture. With more tools, the variety of tasks Bob can do would be even greater.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We’re using Snapchat Spectacles as our hardware and Gemini Live as our base model: the Spectacles stream video and audio data to a Python-built WebSocket server. On initial connection, we establish a new WebSocket connection to Gemini Live and store all subsequent audio and video frames in the session. Asynchronous workers handle buffering uploads, processing responses, executing tool calls, and resuming Gemini Live sessions efficiently. For tools, we used SMTP to integrate Gmail, YOLOE-11 for object detection via text prompts, the Python Slack SDK to integrate Slack, and Google Generative AI SDK for Google Search and Google Map. When voice activation detects that the user has stopped speaking, Gemini Live returns text and tool calls. These get executed and sent back to the Spectacles to update the overlay and bounding box highlights, guiding users through their project. Finally, we would like to note that all WebSockets connections are reused, minimizing the latency between Spectacles and the server.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Messaging with Gemini Live over WebSocket turned out to be particularly challenging, with bugs in the asynchronous context manager and a demanding manual implementation of retry and bidirectional socket management. In addition, projecting pixel coordinates from the camera frame to the Snap Spectacle for object detection required debugging complex coordinate transformations. We solved these issues through test-driven development, A/B testing, and binary search.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: As far as we know, we made the first pair of AR glasses with a multimodal AI agent that can talk back and forth with the user and instruct them in completing physical tasks. Although smart glasses exist, they are incapable of maintaining coherence over a physical task while accepting real-time input, often relying on obtrusive UI like buttons. By integrating live, multimodal agent and object detection into Snap Spectacles, we turned AR glasses into an agent with memory that helps anyone build whatever they want. We’re especially proud of getting the Spectacles to work since none of us had touched AR glasses before this project.

sections.text: Developing AR applications with Lens Studio Working with live instead of turn-based agents State management for WebSocket

sections.heading: What's next for Bob
sections.text: When we interviewed our users about what else they would like to do with Bob, they gave really creative answers: cooking, first aid, martial arts…While these tasks are far from our original goal, Bob can quickly adapt to them because of its agentic framework. Every new tool can unlock a new field for Bob. For example, if we had added Composio’s toolset, Bob would be able to manage your calendar, send Slack messages, and read Notion pages. We could even link Bob to a humanoid robot that collaborates with the user on physical tasks. The future path for Bob is to become the orchestrator directing tens, hundreds or even thousands of humans at a time concurrently on large projects. Managing and monitoring all of them towards common goals while maintaining a common state across workers which would allow for effective collaboration. In addition, Bob is limited by its base models. If we had the hardware, we would run Qwen 2.5-Omni locally to reduce latency and use GroundingDINO to detect objects with greater accuracy.

sections.text: Through steps of labelling, inference, tool call, and execution, Fluffy aims to better the user's experience the best way that it can. Fluffy first labels each object and person in the view with respect to a reference frame (right door, left wall, etc.), then it assigns ownership and relative position based on its labelling with Perceptron's Mk 1.5 VLM. Next, Fluffy infers the next step to do based on the context of the situation both verbally and visually. Ex: person scratching his throat and coughing -> he probably wants water. From this inference, the model makes a tool call depending on the previous inference. We had a set number of tool calls like text, play song, dim lights, open windows, notify caretaker, etc. Execution is the final step where Fluffy executes its series of tool calls and waits for a response for the user. Since this is a continuous stream of data, Fluffy is mostly in the waiting stage, always searching for the correct context to help the user.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built our entire codebase using only Cursor. Our planning was mostly based on research papers of cascading instinctive models and how they behave as well as how modern smart homes execute their tasks. We also made use of the APIs provided in the DubHacks Discord server and Hacker Guide (Spotify API and Photon API) to play music and send emergency texts. Since we were vying for the Perceptron robotics track, we already had the Mk 1.5 in our vision of an ideal Fluffy, but the lack of arm changed our direction from grasping objects for delivery to just an agent meant to assist elderly folks with Perceptron's VLM capabilities.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Cursor was an unfamiliar agent to both of us, and we were unfamiliar with the application before Saturday. Additionally, because SpaceX was unable to provide their free $25 Grok voice credits, our original plan of Mk 1.5 scene description + Grok voice -> Grok reasoning/inference -> API tool calls & execution changed to a Mk 1.5 inference, which gave us less computational awareness, since Mk 1.5 is a lighter model. Additionally, the Mk 1.5 transcribing ability was extremely slow for our purposes, so we had to switch to a Chrome speech-to-text program. Also, one of our team members got his GitHub account banned half-way through coding (oopsies) and the other ran out of Cursor credits so our programming capabilities were slightly impaired around 2AM Sunday, but we persevered.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Being relatively new to the scene of hackathons, we are both very proud that we managed to stay up the whole night and devote our utmost focus onto this project. Moreover, we were able efficiently utilize the hackathon tools through planning and scaffolding our project. This is something that we struggled with in our past hackathons (and just projects in general), and finally being able to realize 'planning' became a very integral part of our hackathon journey at DubHacks.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned how to utilize with agentic workflow through the persistent use of cursor. During the night, we had, at times, 8 agents running simultaneously. With our planning, we were able to properly designate tasks to these agents, helping us work efficiently and successfully.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: At 10 pm on the first night, we had two ideas and no decision. We wrote a design doc for each, half-built a demo for each, and every time one of us pitched, the other two pulled out their phones to check whether it was done. It usually had. We realized we kept going back to whichever project we had sunk the most hours into, and none of us could look things up and argue at the same time. We looked at the AI meeting tools first. All of them are competent secretaries: they transcribe, they summarize, they send you the action items. None of them will sit in the meeting and think with you. We wanted a teammate who would sit in that meeting with us, take the notes, do the research while we talked, and tell us when we were about to rebuild someone else's project. So we built Heard!, the thing we wished had been in the room.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Heard! is an ambient agent teammate that sits in a working meeting. It writes down the ideas and the threads of discussion, looks things up, brings information to the table, answers questions, and joins the discussion when it has something to add. Takes the meeting notes, live, as people talk. Sorts what comes up — ideas, projects, points of discussion — into cards on a shared board. Investigates when needed: researches an open question and brings back supporting information and options. Speaks up when it should, joining the discussion with an opinion of its own. Answers questions from the room, in real time.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We started from the demo, 、wrote out the two-minute meeting we wanted Heard! to sit in, worked backward from what had to happen on screen and when. The first thing we measured was speed. We benchmarked Nemotron models on NVIDIA NIM with reasoning on and off, and the numbers set the design: a card has to be on the board within five seconds of someone naming an idea, so nothing slow can be on that path. Next we designed the architecture from the measurements. A fast Nemotron classifier (Super 120B, reasoning off) reads every few seconds of speech and sorts it: new idea, question, someone talking to Heard. A second Nemotron agent runs in the background and rewrites the meeting notes every twenty seconds. A Claude front desk, running as one long-lived Claude Agent SDK session, makes every decision the room can hear: answer, dispatch a research sub-agent, or stay quiet. Speech in and out is ElevenLabs, Scribe v2 for transcription, and streamed TTS for the voice. Then we built the harness because the model always tries to say something, which is annoying during a real meeting. Finally, we wrote most of the code with Claude Code and tested the whole pipeline. During development, humans wrote most of the docs, architecture designs, implementation specs, and locked down code behavior with tests, while Claude Code implemented the code.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: It's all about ideas. We keep pushing back ideas and coming up with new ones with our own biases. But we are proud that we finally turned this big challenge into the whole project.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are surprised that the NVIDIA Nemotron classifier works so well that during our testing, most of the unrelated chats and debugging chats are well filtered out, and the AI agent doesn't respond to those at all! But everything related to a real project discussion, decision-making, and new ideas is all correctly flagged and recorded. We are proud of the response speed Heard! has. We can reach near real-time asking and answering questions, investigating, and getting a reasonable result in 30s, Nothing to the codebase itself, but our previous AI harnessing experiences make the whole project extremely easy to implement and very robust.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Learned to use Nemotron APIs and ElevenLabs from scratch. Learned to use the Claude Code SDK. Dive deeper into agent loops and architecture design for an agentic system.

sections.heading: What's next for Heard!
sections.text: Maybe persist past memories and make a personal database for all the meeting histories. Potentially rewrite and refine the project to publish as open-source software. Build start-ups that actually solve people's needs.

devpost_page.tagline: LoadCheck helps owner-operator truck drivers uncover the true profit behind every load, build better routes, and prevent cash shortfalls before the wheels move.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Independent owner-operator truck drivers often receive load offers through texts, emails, and screenshots and must decide quickly whether a job is worth accepting. The advertised dollars per mile can look profitable, but that number may leave out deadhead miles, fuel, maintenance, fixed operating costs, dispatcher fees, and upcoming bills. We created LoadCheck because a load that looks good on paper can leave a driver with very little actual profit—or even create a cash shortage before payment arrives. We wanted to give drivers one place to answer a practical question: Should I accept this load, negotiate a better rate, skip it, or build a stronger route?

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: LoadCheck turns a basic load offer into a complete trip decision. A driver can paste an offer or upload a screenshot. Gemini extracts information such as the pickup location, destination, rate, mileage, and delivery times. Before any calculations happen, the driver receives an editable confirmation screen to correct or approve the extracted information. After confirmation, LoadCheck: Calculates the load’s true estimated profit after expenses Includes loaded and empty miles in the analysis Compares the advertised rate with the true net rate Suggests a counteroffer based on the driver’s target profit Searches combinations of up to three loads Considers pickup windows, delivery deadlines, driving limits, and rest periods Identifies stronger home-to-home routes Combines trip expenses with upcoming bills to predict cash shortages Shows whether a delivery advance could keep the trip funded Instead of only showing numbers, LoadCheck explains what those numbers mean and gives the driver a clear next step.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built the frontend with React and TypeScript , creating separate interfaces for offer confirmation, profitability results, route comparison, and the cash-flow timeline. Our backend uses FastAPI and Python . We separated the main calculations into dedicated modules: profit.py calculates load economics and counteroffers optimizer.py searches for feasible multi-load routes cashflow.py simulates balances, expenses, bills, and advances geo.py estimates mileage and caches location data We used Gemini to read unstructured offers and explain completed results in plain language. However, Gemini does not control the financial calculations. Every number shown to the driver comes from deterministic Python code. We also integrated the Capital One Nessie API to supply sandbox banking activity, upcoming bills, and advance information. Cached cities, recorded sandbox data, and offline map support help keep the main demo functional if an external service becomes unavailable.

sections.heading: Challenges we faced
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was extracting consistent information from load offers because they can appear in many formats. Screenshots may have missing labels, shortened city names, or information arranged differently. We addressed this by requiring the driver to confirm and edit the extracted fields before calculations begin. Another challenge was separating AI-generated explanations from reliable financial calculations. We wanted the convenience of AI without allowing it to invent mileage, costs, or profit. Our solution was to let AI handle extraction and explanation while pure Python functions handle every calculation. Route optimization was also challenging because the best-paying loads do not always form a realistic trip. We had to account for pickup windows, delivery deadlines, travel time, empty miles, simplified hours-of-service limits, and whether the route returned the driver home. Finally, combining profitability with cash flow required us to distinguish between earning money eventually and having enough money to complete the trip today . A trip may be profitable overall but still become impossible if a major bill arrives before the carrier pays the driver.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that good AI integration is not about giving AI control over every part of a product. It is about choosing where AI is useful and where predictable code is safer. We also learned that profitability and cash flow are different problems. Calculating that a driver will earn money is not enough if the driver cannot afford fuel, food, or a truck payment while waiting to be paid. From a technical perspective, we gained experience connecting a React frontend to a FastAPI backend, processing image-based input, designing optimization logic, integrating external APIs, and creating fallbacks for unreliable services.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We are proud that LoadCheck connects several decisions that are usually handled separately. It can read an offer, verify its details, calculate its true value, find a stronger route, and identify a possible cash shortage in one workflow. We are also proud of making the system transparent. LoadCheck clearly labels simulated and sandbox information and explains its assumptions, including estimated road mileage, average driving speed, and simplified hours-of-service rules. To validate the project, we completed: 100 passing backend tests 15 out of 15 end-to-end demo checks Testing with 60 simulated load-board offers A three-load route search designed to complete in under one second

sections.heading: What's next for LoadCheck
sections.text: Our next step would be to replace estimated mileage with live commercial-routing data and expand the hours-of-service model to include more federal regulations. We would also like to connect LoadCheck to real load boards, fuel-price services, accounting platforms, and authorized banking data. Long term, LoadCheck could learn a driver’s preferred routes, operating costs, home-time goals, and risk tolerance. This would allow it to provide more personalized recommendations while keeping the final decision in the driver’s hands. LoadCheck helps owner-operators make the decision before the wheels move.

devpost_page.tagline: A stroke can take away your words. Saykind helps you find them again: see a word, hear it slowly, say it, then use it in the real world, with in-app simulations and real-world support.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: About 10 years ago, my (Piyush's) grandfather had a stroke. Overnight, a man who always had something to say had to fight for every word. I watched the frustration up close: knowing exactly what you want to say, and not being able to get it out. What stayed with me even more was his courage. He worked at his recovery every day, and once he had found his words again, he spent his time helping other stroke survivors find theirs. He lived seven more years after his stroke, and he made them count. He has since passed away, but his journey is the reason Saykind exists. I studied data science because I love technology, but my passion has always been healthcare, and today I work as a data engineer in healthcare. Saykind is my team's attempt to do what he did: help people on the same road, with the tools we know best. The numbers show how many people are on that road. Almost 12 million people have a stroke every year, and about 1 in 3 stroke survivors develop aphasia, a language disorder that affects speaking, understanding, reading and writing. That's roughly $$12\text{ million} \times \tfrac{1}{3} \approx 4\text{ million people a year}$$ (our own rough estimate, combining two sources, not a published figure). In a Copenhagen study, 61% of people with aphasia after a stroke still had it a year later. Aphasia takes away words, not intelligence. Sources: World Stroke Organization, Global Stroke Fact Sheet 2025 ; RELEASE Collaborators, Stroke, 2021 ; Pedersen et al., Cerebrovascular Di

sections.text: Saykind is a calm place for adults with aphasia to practice everyday words, then use them in a real conversation. It runs in the browser like a phone app, with nothing to install. sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Speech recognition isn't built for aphasic speech. It mishears fragments and can invent words, so it never judges the person. Saykind shows what it heard, with a caveat, and offers to try again, listen again, or move on. Making vision feel live. Our first camera loop took about 2.6 seconds per frame. Switching to Perceptron's native box mode with reasoning off brought it under about 1.2 seconds. Asking for less made it faster. A real phone broke our layout. On an iPhone, the microphone panel covered the word. We rebuilt both Level 1 screens as three rows, with the panel pinned to the bottom. Tone is harder than it looks. A prompt alone wasn't enough, so we built a phrase filter plus rules, covering the barista, the hints, the report and the screen text. Reports must never fail. Any model error, missing key or blocked wording falls back to a fixed template. Free-plan limits. Our first ElevenLabs voice required a paid plan, so we switched to a premade voice and wrote a clear error message for that case.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Many people struggle with receiving timely dermatological care due to barriers such as high medical costs, limited availability of professionals, and time constraints. Skin-related conditions, if left untreated, can worsen over time, leading to severe complications. Inspired by this gap in accessibility, we set out to build an AI-powered solution that provides users with an instant and preliminary skin condition assessment using computer vision. Our goal is to empower individuals to take control of their skin health while making dermatological advice more accessible and efficient.

sections.text: SkinGuard is an AI-driven dermatologist assistant designed to help users analyze their skin conditions instantly. The platform allows users to upload pictures of their skin, which our AI model processes to predict possible conditions. Additionally, an AI-powered chatbot is available to provide explanations, suggest solutions, and answer related queries. To encourage continuous monitoring, SkinGuard also includes a skin tracker feature, allowing users to log and track changes over time for better long-term assessment and treatment.

devpost_page.title: SideQuests
devpost_page.tagline: Turn waiting into wandering: tell SideQuests your free window and mood, and get a timed plan of nearby events and places, with transit, that you can open up for others to join.

sections.text: SideQuests Turn waiting into wandering. Tell SideQuests where you are, when you need to be back and what you're in the mood for. It builds a timed plan of nearby events and places, with the travel between them, that fits your taste. The plan gets better every time you rate an outing, and you can open it up for people nearby to join. Note: for information about our HEARSAY submission, please scroll to the bottom!

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Three of us (Bayan, Kevin and Karthik) met on a study-abroad program this summer, and Max has plenty of his own travel stories. We kept running into the same problem: free time in a place we didn't know, and no fast way to turn it into something worth doing. Bayan in Belgium: they asked what to do and the internet said "eat waffles." They found some overpriced, mediocre waffles, saw a couple of tourist attractions a local suggested, then went straight back to the train station because nothing else came to mind. Max's layovers: in France, he and his mom planned a transit-only day with ChatGPT and got a generic list with no timing or routes. In Vienna, he and his dad wanted schnitzel and sightseeing. They took badly ordered routes, reached the sights after dark, and found every kitchen closed. Karthik in Berlin: he found that he loves travel when it fits him: nature and small groups in the Tiergarten, plus the city's social events. A generic "top 10" list would never have found that mix. All summer: we organized trips in the most decentralized way possible: across a travel app, a calendar, a group chat and two payment apps. We knew there had to be something better. Google Maps, ChatGPT, Fever, Wanderlog and meetup apps like WashedUp each cover one piece. However, none of them carry the whole package. SideQuests turns events, places and transit into one timed plan, learns from your ratings, and lets others join until the plan locks.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Taste onboarding: you rate ten interests from 1 to 5, set your company, pace and spend, and answer three short prompts. You can also import your likes from Facebook, which the app turns into suggested ratings for you to approve. From all of this, we build a likes embedding and a dislikes embedding. A sidequest in about 30 seconds: pick where you start and end, how far you'll go, and when you need to be back, then type or dictate your mood ("chill and outside, then live music"). In 0.2–0.6 s you get three timed plans with the walk, transit or rideshare legs between stops. Drag to reorder and the route re-times itself. Press and hold a stop to swap it for something similar. Social: keep a plan private, share it with friends, or post it to the Forum with a group-size cap and a lock time. You can also post that you're free right now. Every group gets a chat, a shared photo album and an expense split that's exact to the cent. Updates arrive live over WebSockets. Agentic checkout: for ticketed activities, an agent finds tickets on the official site, fills in your details, waits for your approval (or buys instantly under a limit you set) and books them. The ticket then appears on that stop for everyone in the group. The feedback loop: you rate each stop after the outing, and those ratings update your taste profile, so your next plan starts smarter.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Three contracts. The app, the backend and the ML work were built separately and didn't agree on formats. We made the app the source of truth and enforced it with generated examples and strict contract tests. No users, no labels. We generated realistic noisy data and judged it with an LLM, using disjoint splits so the metrics mean something. Embedding drift. A single instruction prefix would have silently broken the classifier, so we built the parity gate. Boring plans. Early plans had one or two stops. Letting people join events late, adding a quality bar for stops and running the diagnosis rounds raised them to three or four. Time. Time zones, windows that run past midnight, and a demo that works on any day.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Plans with hard guarantees in under a second. A live, deployed system with a real 9,000-activity catalog and a seeded demo world. An app that feels like a product.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Putting everything in one text format mattered more than model architecture. Retrieval, ranking and planning are three different problems, and you need all three. Synthetic data needs as much rigor as real data. Log every decision the model makes, because those logs are tomorrow's training data.
